United States Army Communications Technology · Historical Survey · By: Zacc Rittman

Communication Technology
Shaping the Battlefield

A chronological survey of major communications technologies fielded and/or developed by the U.S. Army. A description of how each era exposed technological shortcomings and how the next generation of technology addressed them.

01
World War II
1939 – 1945
1940
SCR-300 — The First True Walkie-Talkie
Portable Radio
A 32–38 lb FM backpack radio that gave infantry platoons real-time voice contact with headquarters for the first time.
Description
The “Signal Corps Radio” 300, or “walkie-talkie,” was created between 1940 and 1942. An infantry-portable radio, allowing almost instantaneous communication between frontline troops, and their headquarters elements. It was a portable frequency modulated transmitter and receiver radio. The unit used glass vacuum tubes to amplify signals allowing the user to hear transmissions.[1,4] It weighed between 32 and 38 pounds and had a 20–25 hour battery life.[1] Its combat debut came in Southern Italy where it performed exceptionally despite its quirks like a ten minute “warm-up” period or not being completely waterproof.[4] The SCR-300 was essential for success during D-Day and the Battle of the Bulge.[1,2,4]

1941
SCR-536 — The Handie-Talkie
Portable Radio
A 5 lb one-hand AM radio carried by rifle company leaders — the ancestor of every modern handheld two-way radio.
Description
Weighing in at five pounds, the SCR-536, or “handie-talkie,” started development in 1940 by Don Mitchell of Galvin Manufacturing (precursor to Motorola). They used glass vacuum tubes with a water resistant casing.[1] Its battery life was less than 24 hours of normal use and units were turned on by extending the large 40-inch antenna.[1,2] One downside of this platform was the inability to make “field adjustments.” The 536 was limited to a single channel which needed to be adjusted at the division-level radio shop.[2] Additionally, many soldiers complained about units leaking water and failing, notably during amphibious landings at Operation Torch and D-Day.[2] It entered mass production in 1941 with Galvin Manufacturing ultimately producing approximately 130,000 units.[1]

While the second world war proved the effectiveness and necessity of tactical radios, it also demonstrated shortcomings of 1940s technology. Glass vacuum tubes meant radios were heavy and fragile. They operated on a single channel and were unencrypted. In the post-war period, some of these issues were addressed by miniaturization programs and the invention of transistors. These programs paralleled the burgeoning space race which drove the Signal Corps toward Project Diana and early satellite communications. Vietnam was a test bed of these new technologies and is the true intersection point between electronics and radio signals.

02
Cold War & Vietnam
1946 – 1979
1946
Project Diana — Moon Bounce Radar
Satellite / Space
The first successful Earth–Moon–Earth radar contact, proving radio waves could penetrate the ionosphere and opening the door to satellite communications.
Description
This was the Signal Corps' first attempt at extraterrestrial radio communications. On January 10th, 1946, from Fort Monmouth, New Jersey they used a modified SCR-271 radar set from WWII to bounce radar signals off the Moon.[1] The reflected signal returned 2.5 seconds later, having traveled roughly 477,000 miles round trip.[1] The experiment grew out of a desire to detect and track enemy ballistic missiles through the ionosphere.[3] The researchers used the experiment as a proof of concept for satellite communications being able to penetrate the atmosphere. Project Diana led to the Passive Moon Relay (PAMOR) project nicknamed “Joe.” Its goal was to spy on Soviet military communications by picking up signals they were unintentionally bouncing off the Moon.[3]

1952
Transistor & Printed Wiring Board
Data / C2
Two postwar breakthroughs — the transistor and dip-soldered printed wiring — that made miniaturized, ruggedized military electronics possible.
Description
Post-WWII the military understood the importance of radios being carried by frontline soldiers. One inhibiting factor was their size and weight. WWII-era radios used large and heavy glass vacuum tubes to amplify and switch electrical signals.[1] The Army began a widespread push to “miniaturize” new technology. For this purpose, the Signal Corps invented dip-soldered printed wiring in 1948.[1] This enabled manufacturers to produce more high-density components instead of manually soldered connections. Bell Labs invented the electric transistor in late 1947, which replaced the heavy glass vacuum tubes and directed electricity more efficiently.[2]

1958
Project SCORE — First Communications Satellite
Satellite / Space
The world's first purpose-built communications satellite, which broadcast President Eisenhower's Christmas message — the first human voice transmitted from space.
Description
Project SCORE marks the culmination of Project Diana. Constructed by the Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA, precursor to DARPA), SCORE was the first purpose-built communications satellite in the world.[1] It was launched from Cape Canaveral, Florida on December 18, 1958.[1] They estimated its orbital lifetime to be 34 days and they experimented on the satellite for twelve.[1] While in orbit ARPA agents uploaded President Eisenhower's Christmas Greeting. When it was played only extremely sensitive receivers picked it up, so the message was relayed to the general public over normal radio stations.[1,3]

1962
BACKPORCH Troposcatter Radio Network
Network
A tropospheric scatter system that bounced radio signals off the upper atmosphere to bypass Vietnam's jungle canopy, extending range up to 500 km.
Description
The Vietnamese geography did not lend itself well to effective radio communications, especially communications beyond line of sight (BLOS). The thick jungle absorbed and scattered radio signals, making reliable communication nearly impossible.[1,4] To solve this issue the Signal Corps leveraged new troposcatter technology defined as radio signals “beamed up into the atmosphere” and “bounced back down to Earth with good results, bypassing debilitating terrain.”[1] Using troposcatter, the effective range of some high-power radios found in communication outposts was upwards of 500 kilometers.[2]

1963
AUTOVON — Automated Voice Network
Network
The military's worldwide automated telephone network with priority-based call preemption — a precursor to modern redundant network routing.
Description
AUTOVON, or Automated Voice Network, which the Army installed in 1963, created a long distance calling system.[1] It was a major component of the Defense Communications System (DCS) and stretched from the states to allied European countries. It consisted of AT&T-installed circuits and phone lines.[1] The biggest differentiator between the burgeoning civilian phone line infrastructure and AUTOVON was “message precedence levels.” Civilian phone lines became “busy” upon receiving too many calls, whereas AUTOVON would disconnect lower priority calls if a higher priority message was coming through.[1,4] The precedence levels were as follows: priority, immediate, flash, and flash override.[1] AUTOVON pioneered many communications advancements like using three-digit area codes and routing calls using a “polygrid” system. The polygrid was non-hierarchical and designed to survive nodes being destroyed and foreshadowed the redundant routing design that would later characterize Internet protocols.[4]

1966
AN/PRC-25 / AN/PRC-77 FM Manpack Radios
Portable Radio
The workhorse radios of Vietnam — the PRC-25 introduced solid-state circuitry, and its successor the PRC-77 added voice encryption for the first time.
Description
The AN/PRC-25, affectionately nicknamed the “prick-25,” was the most widely used radio in Vietnam with manufacturers producing approximately 130,000 units.[1,2] It incorporated pioneering solid-state circuitry which made it water resistant.[2] It came in two components: the upper transceiver and lower battery pack. Similar to most infantry-portable radios, it came with two antennas, a standard three foot antenna, and a ten foot long range antenna.[2] The PRC-25 was lighter than its WWII counterpart weighing between 24–25 pounds.[1] Its upgraded version, the AN/PRC-77 or “prick-77,” was introduced to soldiers in 1968.[4] The 77 brought two major upgrades to infantry-portable radios. The first improvement replaced the final power amplification stage of the design with a transistor-based version. The transistor made the 77 lighter and more power-efficient.[4] The second improvement was the implementation of voice encryption using the KY-38 NESTOR then KY-57 VINSON systems. These systems converted analog voice transmissions into digital signals which were then encrypted.[4]

1966
Integrated Wideband Communications System (IWCS)
Network
A three-phase expansion of BACKPORCH into a theater-wide microwave and troposcatter backbone supporting up to 400,000 troops across Southeast Asia.
Description
The Integrated Wideband Communications System's goal was to expand the BACKPORCH system incrementally into Thailand and Vietnam, which would become the Southeast Asia portion of the Defense Communication System (DCS).[3] IWCS' implementation was split into three phases. First was to expand the existing BACKPORCH hardware. Phase I was intended for 40,000 troops but significant delays of up to two years, meant that when the first phase I circuit was installed U.S. strength exceeded 350,000 troops.[3] Phase II upgraded existing IWCS sites and installed new ones close to the frontline. All in all this phase supported 200,000 soldiers despite tripling the circuit total. Finally, the culmination of IWCS, phase III, focused on upgrading and installing circuits in the Mekong Delta. Once completed, the full system supported 400,000 troops.[3] Notably, the installations were largely unmolested by Viet Cong forces, though one contractor convoy was ambushed during construction.[2]

1966
First Operational Military Communications Satellite
Satellite / Space
The IDCSP constellation — the DoD's first operational satellite system, enabling real-time battlefield analysis via space-based communications.
Description
The Air Force launched the first seven satellites of the “Initial Defense Communications Satellite Program” in June 1966 marking the DOD's initial foray into satellite constellations.[1] Washington's goal was to deploy global military space-based communications. Initial ground terminals were installed in Saigon and Nha Trang, Vietnam.[1] For the first time, “real-time battlefield analysis” could be conducted from anywhere in the world via high resolution photographs taken by the satellite constellation.[1] The initial program was such a success that by 1968 the fourth system of satellites had been launched. Its largest benefit was acting as a secure global communications channel used for command and control instead of insecure commercial satellites.[1]

All of the new systems worked exceptionally in isolation but lacked integration. Satellites and radios could not interoperate, the wideband network was always behind the troop buildup, and encryption modules were incompatible with most fielded radios. The Army understood that individual radios were better than no radios, but that the future lay in integrated networks. Networks would give everyone a common operational understanding leading to battlefield success. This mirrored the same networking revolution happening in the civilian world and drove investment into technologies like mobile subscriber equipment and SINCGARS.

03
Information Age
1980 – 1999
1983
SINCGARS — Single Channel Ground and Airborne Radio System
Portable Radio
A frequency-hopping VHF combat radio that cycles through 100+ frequencies per second — still in frontline service over 40 years later.
Description
Introduced in 1983, the Single Channel Ground and Airborne Radio System replaced the Vietnam-era AN/PRC-77 but remained backwards compatible.[1] The radio operated in three configurations: ground, maritime, and airborne. It is intentionally modular so parts are easy to repair, recycle, and upgrade.[1] It can operate in single channel or encrypted/frequency hopping mode. In frequency-hopping mode, the radio cycles through frequencies over one hundred times per second, making jamming and interception far more difficult.[1,3] Multiple power settings allow operators to adjust range from 200 meters to ten kilometers and minimize their electromagnetic signature.[1] The platform is so successful the Army invested in three “enhancement rounds.” The integrated communications security upgrade brought encryption to the SINCGARS and then the special improvement program (SIP) and advanced SIP made the SINCGARS smaller and half its original weight.[1]

1988
Mobile Subscriber Equipment (MSE)
Network
A truck-mounted cellular-style network that gave mobile units automatic call routing — the 93rd Signal Brigade's MSE spanned 29,000 sq mi in Desert Storm.
Description
First fielded in 1988, mobile subscriber equipment (MSE) was the precursor to modern day civilian phone networks.[1] It provided better range, error correction, data capability, and automatic call routing when compared to Vietnam-era field telephone systems. MSE relied on radio signals to switch users instead of manually-operated switchboxes.[1] The military understood that the network needed to be scalable and mobile. Instead of building communications towers and stations as in Vietnam, MSE used truck mounted hardware.[1,2] The mobile network sent “packet-based” voice communications and was critical to Allied success in the first Gulf War because the 93rd Signal Brigade and 3rd Armored Division chained together MSE trucks to grow with the frontline. The signal brigade's network ended up spanning nearly 29,000 square miles within Kuwait.[1]

1990
EPLRS — Enhanced Position Location Reporting System
Data / C2
A tactical data distribution network that calculated user positions from radio signal timing — a precursor to GPS-based tracking on the battlefield.
Description
The enhanced position location reporting system predated widespread GPS adoption and provided an early form of automated position reporting.[1] Within the mobile network, each user, or node, would send data through their radios. The reporting system then records how long it takes each node to reply to the data. Using that time it can then calculate the position of the user's radio.[1] The EPLRS systems were installed on each allied vehicle and used to update battle maps and blue force trackers.[1]

The first Gulf War showed the effectiveness of networked systems. As of 2026, it is the last American war pitting two conventional forces against each other. Desert Storm had clear frontlines, but most importantly, each unit was not far from their higher headquarters. During the Global War on Terror warfare fundamentally changed from large units moving across the desert, to small patrols moving through villages expecting contact from all around. The Army realized frontline soldiers needed to communicate not just with their headquarters but air support as well. The Army pushed communications capabilities down to the lowest level with ATAK and the Rifleman Radio. Most recently, instead of driving commercial innovation, the DoD started adopting existing platforms like Android phones and Starlink satellite constellations.

04
GWOT & Modern Era
2000 – Present
2003
Blue Force Tracking (BFT)
Data / C2
GPS-enabled vehicle tracking that displays friendly and enemy positions on a digital map — reducing fratricide to historic lows.
Description
Blue Force Tracking (BFT) encompasses many technologies beginning from a field test in 1997 known as Task Force XXI. The first large scale BFT was the “Force XXI Battle Command Brigade and Below.”[1,3] FBCB2 used its own network and forwarded all information to an associated tactical operations center (TOC). It leveraged both SINCGARS and EPLRS to display on a screen where the user's vehicle was.[3] Soldiers could mark enemy positions, plan routes, and send data all on a digital screen. Northrop Grumman was contracted to produce 160,000 units because the system reduced fratricide to all-time-low levels.[1,2]

2004
WIN-T Increment 1 — Warfighter Information Network-Tactical
Network
The MSE's replacement — an IP-based tactical network linking theaters down to battalions via satellite and semi-fixed command posts.
Description
The Warfighter Information Network-Tactical replaced the MSE.[1,2] The first increment implemented the internet protocol, or IP, links for theaters down to battalions. WIN-T used a network of semi-fixed command posts and satellites to manage everything from blue force tracking to calling down artillery.[1] It marked a fundamental shift away from phone lines (wired or wireless) toward IP-based communication.[2]

2010
ATAK — Android Team Awareness Kit
Data / C2
A DARPA-developed Android app that turns a phone into a command platform — blue force tracking, targeting, and artillery calls in one device.
Description
ATAK, standing for Android Team Awareness Kit, struggled to gain traction within the military community because of its unassuming appearance. The kit converts an Android phone into a combination of many useful tools like an integrated blue force tracker and the ability to call in artillery.[1,3] Originally, DARPA intended just to create a robust information sharing platform, but they ended up making a modular, lightweight, all-in-one situational awareness and command platform.[2] Impressively, ATAK is now being integrated with everything via plugins to give each soldier an accurate real-time picture of the battlefield.[1]

2012
WIN-T Increment 2 — Networking on the Move
Network
Extended WIN-T to company level with vehicle-mounted hardware that maintains connectivity on the move — no more stopping to set up relay stations.
Description
This increment extends the Warfighter Information Network down to the Company-level. Introduced in 2012, it added support for vehicle-based hardware.[1,2] The biggest advantage compared to increment one is the ability of vehicles to maintain their network while moving, as opposed to stopping and setting up stations.[2] The second generation implemented a “point of presence” system which allowed vehicles to discover and automatically integrate new nodes into the network.[2] Company commanders had a more granular view of their forces similar to that of a Battalion or Brigade commander.[1]

2014
AN/PRC-154 Rifleman Radio
Portable Radio
An intra-squad handheld radio enabling every member of a rifle squad to communicate via voice and data, forming a mesh network with 50 km range.
Description
Army designers returned to form with this invention harking back to the “handie-talkie.” The AN/PRC-154 serves a radically different purpose. It is meant to act as an intra-squad tactical radio carried by all members of a rifle squad.[1] Squad and team leaders are now able to speak with their entire unit at a distance instead of relying purely on hand and arm signals. The 154 has a standard range of two kilometers and a battery life of approximately ten hours.[1,2] It can extend its range to 50 kilometers by forming a mesh network between ground radios and nearby UAVs or aircraft carrying the same system.[2] Occasionally, this allows the platoon leader to leave behind the heavier manpack radios.[2]

Commercial LEO Satellite Integration (Starlink / Starshield)
Satellite / Space
The Army's pilot program testing SpaceX's Starlink and Starshield for tactical broadband — leveraging commercial satellite constellations for military use.
Description
The Army has begun researching and testing SpaceX's low-Earth orbiting satellite constellations, Starlink and its military counterpart Starshield.[1] The main advantages these systems have over military-operated satellites are faster broadband and data transfer speeds. Ideally the Army will begin integrating Starshield technology into older satellite command (SATCOM) hardware.[1]

2025
Unified Network & Zero Trust Architecture
Network
The DoD's plan to merge all tactical networks into a single Zero Trust platform — integrating 5G, AI, and quantum-resistant cryptography by 2028.
Description
At the beginning of the 2020s, the concept of a “Unified Network” (UNO) became one of the DoD's primary focuses.[2] It aims to integrate previous platforms like WIN-T with modern advancements such as “5G, software-defined networking (SDN), artificial intelligence (AI), and quantum-resistant cryptography.”[2] Unlike civilian networks, the UNO will use a “Zero Trust” model. Traditional networks have perimeter-based defenses, whereas ZTA requires continuous authentication of not only users, but devices as well.[1] The DoD targets 2028 for the implementation of its single, cutting-edge, and secure global network.[2]

The Army's Greatest Weapon

Communications technology has given the American military unprecedented force multiplication in all conflicts since WWII. Each technological leap solved flaws identified by earlier conflicts from portability to security. Communications technology continues to evolve rapidly and it is important that the U.S. Army is at the forefront of innovation. Since the mid-20th century its most important weapon is not firearms or vehicles, but keeping everyone informed and communicative. The means by which that happens is communications technology, whether that occurs via a handheld radio or Starlink satellite.
